title: Volatility
subtitle: A measure of how much an asset's price swings over time
openingQuestion: Stock A swings 2-3% per day, stock B swings 0.3-0.5% per day. Which stock has higher volatility?
openingOptions: Cannot be determined without knowing the observation period
Both are equal if their ending price is the same
Stock A - volatility measures the magnitude of price swings, and A swings far more, so its volatility is higher
explanation: Volatility measures how much an asset's price swings over time, usually calculated as the standard deviation of returns. High volatility isn't necessarily bad - it simply reflects a degree of uncertainty, and it usually comes with higher potential return as compensation for that uncertainty.

diagram.label: An asset's price swings over time
Measured by the standard deviation of returns

realWorldExample.description: High-growth tech stocks (like newly listed startups) usually have very high volatility, while public utility stocks (electricity, water) tend to be stable, with much lower volatility.

quiz.question: Does high volatility always mean 'bad risk' that should be avoided?
options: Yes, high volatility always lowers long-term returns
No, it amplifies both gains and losses
Yes, because institutional investors always avoid volatile assets
No, because volatility has no effect on expected return
quiz.explanation: Volatility is a double-edged sword: it amplifies both large gains and large losses. A young investor with a long time horizon may accept high volatility in exchange for a higher expected return; an investor near retirement usually prefers low volatility to preserve accumulated capital.

quiz.question: A stock's volatility measured over the past 3 months is very low. Does that guarantee the next 3 months will also stay low?
options: Yes, as long as the company discloses nothing unusual
Yes, volatility is a fixed, stable trait of each asset
No, volatility can spike suddenly when an unexpected event hits
No, because volatility always reverses every three months
quiz.explanation: This is an important limit of every measure based on historical data: volatility can spike suddenly (volatility clustering) when an unexpected event hits - a long calm stretch is sometimes actually a warning sign of a sharp move ahead, not a guarantee of long-term stability.

quiz.question: What does volatility clustering mean?
options: A portfolio's volatility equals the sum of each asset's own volatility
Assets in the same industry always end up with identical volatility
Volatility concentrates at the start and end of each trading session
A period of strong volatility tends to be followed by more volatility
quiz.explanation: Markets don't move randomly from calm to chaotic and back to calm - shocks arrive in clusters. This is why low volatility over the past three months is no guarantee the next three will be low too.

quiz.question: Why can a young investor accept higher volatility than someone close to retirement?
options: Because they have time to wait for the market to recover
Because their higher income makes them tolerate losses better
Because highly volatile assets always deliver higher returns
Because they get a tax break for investing longer-term
quiz.explanation: Volatility only becomes a permanent loss when you're forced to sell while the market is down. A long time horizon allows you to wait; someone withdrawing money within the next three years doesn't have that option.

quiz.question: Two funds both average 10%/year, one with 8% volatility and one with 25%. What's the real-world difference?
options: The two funds deliver identical outcomes since their average return is equal
The higher-volatility fund's actual realized outcome is far less steady
The higher-volatility fund is guaranteed to deliver a higher final outcome
The lower-volatility fund has a correspondingly higher management fee
quiz.explanation: Same average, very different paths: the 25%-volatility fund has years where it loses a third of its value. For someone who must withdraw money in exactly that year, the two funds are anything but the same.

keyTakeaways: Volatility: a measure of how much an asset's price swings
High volatility isn't inherently bad - weigh it against expected return and risk tolerance
One of the most important inputs into every portfolio risk-management model

practicePrompt.question: Stock A swings between 90,000 VND and 110,000 VND within a month. Stock B swings between 98,000 VND and 102,000 VND over the same period, even though both end the month at a similar price (around 100,000 VND). What concept describes the difference in how much these two stocks 'dance' in price?
options: This is a difference in Expected Return, since the two stocks have different expected returns
Volatility is a measure of price-swing magnitude; A has a wider range than B
This is a difference in Correlation between the two stocks and the broad market
No financial concept describes this difference between the two stocks
practicePrompt.explanation: Volatility: a measure of how much an asset's price swings. Stock A has higher volatility (a wider range: 90,000-110,000) than B (98,000-102,000) - high volatility usually comes with higher risk even when the final return can look the same.

summary.keyIdea: Volatility: a measure of how much an asset's price swings
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: High volatility isn't inherently bad - weigh it against expected return and risk tolerance

application.title: Compare the volatility of two assets
application.message: Look at the 6-month price chart of a stock and a bond fund, and judge for yourself which line looks 'rougher' - that's the volatility you're sensing visually.
application.secondary: High volatility doesn't mean bad, just that you need to prepare yourself mentally for it.

sections.text: Volatility measures how much an asset's price swings over time, usually calculated as the standard deviation of returns. High volatility isn't automatically a bad thing - it simply reflects a degree of uncertainty, and it usually comes with a higher potential return as compensation for that instability.

Volatility amplifies both the potential for large gains and large losses. High-growth tech stocks (like newly listed startups) usually carry very high volatility, while public utility stocks (electricity, water) are far more stable. A young investor with a long time horizon can accept high volatility in exchange for a higher expected return; someone near retirement usually prioritizes low volatility to preserve the capital they've already accumulated.
Past volatility doesn't guarantee the future

A stock with very low volatility over the past 3 months isn't guaranteed to stay calm for the next 3. Volatility can spike suddenly when an unexpected event hits - bad news, a crisis, a fundamental shift in the business. This is called "volatility clustering": a long calm stretch is sometimes actually a warning sign of a sharp move ahead, not a guarantee of lasting stability.

items: Volatility measures the magnitude of price swings, not their direction (up or down)
High volatility needs a correspondingly higher expected return to be worthwhile
The longer your time horizon, the more high volatility you can reasonably accept
Historical volatility data is only a reference estimate, not a promise about the future

lines: Volatility isn't an investor's enemy - not understanding it is the real enemy.
